# PM Samajik Sahayata Yojana: Evaluating NSAP Reforms and Welfare Architecture


While PM Samajik Sahayata Yojana widens disability aid, frozen ₹200 pensions highlight the growing fiscal burden shifting from the Centre to state governments.

The transition to PM Samajik Sahayata Yojana brings structural updates to disability assistance but leaves baseline old-age pensions at long-frozen levels.


### Overview


The Union Cabinet restructured India's non-contributory welfare net in October 2026 by approving the Pradhan Mantri Samajik Sahayata Yojana with an outlay of **₹53,428 crore** over five years. Yet the reform leaves the central old-age pension frozen at **₹200 per month** for individuals aged 60 to 79.


The initiative is primarily a **nomenclature rationalisation** rather than a structural expansion. While disability criteria are relaxed, static demographic quotas dating back to 2001 still exclude millions of destitute senior citizens. Consequently, the financial burden of fulfilling constitutional welfare mandates falls almost entirely on state exchequers.


## Why in the News: The Shift to PM Samajik Sahayata


The Union Cabinet approved the continuation of the National Social Assistance Programme as the Pradhan Mantri Samajik Sahayata Yojana on 14 October 2026. This administrative overhaul commits an outlay of **₹53,428 crore** covering the five-year period from FY 2026–27 to FY 2030–31.


The scheme unifies several longstanding centrally sponsored schemes under revised titles:


- **Pradhan Mantri Vridhavastha Pension Yojana** : Replaces the Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme.
- **Pradhan Mantri Vidhawa Pension Yojana** : Succeeds the Indira Gandhi National Widow Pension Scheme.
- **Pradhan Mantri Divyangjan Pension Yojana** : Restructures the disability pension component.
- **Pradhan Mantri Parivar Labh Yojana** : Renames the National Family Benefit Scheme, retaining the one-time lump-sum grant of ₹20,000 for bereaved below-poverty-line families.


Beyond nomenclature, the operational framework modifies parameters for persons with disabilities. It lowers the **benchmark disability threshold** and removes **entry-age barriers** . However, baseline cash transfers for the elderly remain unchanged, leading policy analysts to question whether the package delivers genuine welfare reform or cosmetic rebranding.

## The 200-Rupee Trap: Why the Legacy NSAP Architecture Froze in Time


India's baseline old-age pension has remained stagnant for two decades. The Ministry of Rural Development continues to peg central assistance at **₹200 per month** for beneficiaries aged 60 to 79 years.


This amount has remained completely unchanged since the **2006–07 fiscal revision** . Beneficiaries aged 80 and above receive **₹500 per month** , an allocation frozen since 2011.


Key figures illustrate the erosion of this safety net:


- **₹6.66 per day** : The real daily value of a ₹200 monthly transfer, delivering **less than 5%** of national minimum wage benchmarks.
- **Unadjusted for inflation** : Two decades of price increases have hollowed out the real purchasing power of the stipend, failing to meet nutritional or medical needs.
- **₹9,671 crore allocation** : The NSAP allocation in Union Budget 2026–27 accounts for roughly **4% of the budget** of the Department of Rural Development.


Parliamentary committees have repeatedly criticised this stagnation. In its 5th Report for the 18th Lok Sabha, the Standing Committee on Rural Development and Panchayati Raj called the transfer **exceptionally meagre assistance** . The panel recommended an immediate upward revision linked to the **cost-of-living index** , warning that nominal cash transfers without periodic indexation fail to provide social protection.


Frozen at ₹200 since 2006, the central old-age pension has experienced massive purchasing power erosion against inflation over two decades.


## Side-by-Side: What Changes Under PM Samajik Sahayata


The Pradhan Mantri Samajik Sahayata Yojana alters administrative nomenclature and specific disability parameters while leaving old-age transfers static. The central monthly assistance under the newly renamed Pradhan Mantri Divyangjan Pension Yojana increases by **25% from ₹300 to ₹375** for beneficiaries aged 0 to 79 years, and from **₹500 to ₹625** for citizens aged 80 and above.


Eligibility for disability pensions undergoes meaningful reform. The Ministry of Rural Development lowered the **qualifying disability threshold** from 80% to 40% and eliminated the previous minimum age requirement of 18 years, enabling financial support from birth. In contrast, the old-age pension framework retains its legacy rate structure.

## Targeting vs Universal Coverage: Will Dynamic Registries End Exclusion?


Outdated demographic baselines create severe administrative exclusion in the NSAP framework. The Comptroller and Auditor General of India, in Report No. 25 of 2023, pointed out that state quotas remain bound to **Census 2001 population figures** and 2004–05 poverty estimates. These archaic markers ignore a quarter-century of population aging.


Key structural constraints and leakages include:


- **Widening demographic gap** : India's elderly demographic expanded from **7.6 crore in Census 2001** to **10.38 crore in Census 2011** , and is projected to reach **17.3 crore individuals** by 2026.
- **Static national caps** : Lifting the national ceiling from **3.09 crore to 3.20 crore beneficiaries** adds only 11 lakh slots across all schemes combined, leaving millions outside formal coverage.
- **High economic vulnerability** : Data indicates that **over 40% of Indian seniors** occupy the poorest wealth quintile, forcing nearly **half of all elderly men** and **22% of elderly women** to continue manual labour into advanced age.
- **Audit leakages** : CAG Report No. 25 of 2023 uncovered **₹2.0 crore in irregular disbursements** to 2,103 deceased beneficiaries across 26 States and UTs.


Direct Benefit Transfer systems deployed on the NSAP-PPS portal and Public Financial Management System have curtailed ghost beneficiaries since December 2014. Nevertheless, procedural bottlenecks like biometric mismatches continue to lock out genuine, infirm claimants.


While India's elderly population expanded past 17 crore by 2026, the central social assistance cap remained locked near 2001 levels.

## The Fiscal Federalism Divide: State Top-Ups and Central Stagnation


The Seventh Schedule places social security, invalid pensions, and old-age relief under Entries 23 and 24 of the Concurrent List. While legislative jurisdiction is joint, financial obligations have shifted heavily to state governments.


The resulting fiscal distortions manifest in several ways:


- **Disproportionate state financing** : Regional governments now finance between **70% to more than 90%** of total monthly disbursements, contributing top-ups ranging from **₹800 to ₹3,800 per month** over the ₹200 central baseline.
- **Geographic inequity** : Because relief levels depend on state fiscal capacity, citizens with identical physical vulnerabilities receive vastly different support depending on their address.
- **Tighter release conditions** : Starting FY 2024–25, central allocations arrive in four quarterly instalments that are withheld if states fail to upload prompt utilisation certificates and digitised rolls, per the Standing Committee on Rural Development and Panchayati Raj.
- **Inter-scheme fund diversions** : CAG Report No. 25 of 2023 uncovered that **₹57.45 crore of NSAP funds** were diverted across six States and UTs (Bihar, Goa, Odisha, Rajasthan, Chhattisgarh, and Jammu & Kashmir) for unapproved operational costs.


Diversion also occurred at the central level. The Ministry of Rural Development diverted **₹2.83 crore of NSAP funds** intended for administration and publicity to finance campaigns for unrelated schemes like PMAY-G and DDU-GKY. This trend strains cooperative federalism, compelling cash-strapped states to shoulder the social floor alone.

## Constitutional Mandate: Moving from Discretionary Relief to Article 41 Rights


India's non-contributory welfare architecture is grounded in distinct constitutional directives and judicial interpretations:


- **Article 41 of the Constitution** : Establishes a Directive Principle requiring the State to secure public assistance in cases of old age, sickness, and disablement, qualified only by economic capacity.
- **Article 21 guarantees** : In **Ashwani Kumar v. Union of India (2019)** , the Supreme Court ruled that senior citizens possess a fundamental right to **live with dignity under Article 21** , ordering governments to reassess pension amounts and elder-care infrastructure.


Treating public pensions as discretionary executive charity conflicts with this rights-based mandate. A frozen transfer of ₹200 a month reduces social protection to a symbolic gesture. To realise the vision of Articles 21 and 41, India must transition from discretionary handouts to an enforceable statutory safety net.


Judicial interpretation under Article 21 links the state's directive principles under Article 41 directly to the fundamental right to live with dignity.

## Way Forward: Building an Inflation-Indexed Social Protection Floor


The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Rural Development and Panchayati Raj provides a clear institutional blueprint for reforming non-contributory social security. Establishing an effective safety net requires moving away from static nominal grants toward an automated indexation mechanism.


- **Mandatory Cost-of-Living Indexation** : The Union government must revise the frozen ₹200 base rate and link future annual revisions directly to the Consumer Price Index for Agricultural Labourers (CPI-AL), matching the indexation mechanism utilised for rural wage calculations.
- **Dynamic Demography-Linked Caps** : Beneficiary thresholds must decouple from Census 2001 limits. Quotas must be recalibrated against updated population projections, expanding national safety nets to reflect the 17.3 crore elderly citizens documented by the National Commission on Population.
- **Equitable Union-State Cost-Sharing** : The financing architecture must transition toward a statutory 60:40 or 50:50 sharing ratio between the Union and the States, replacing the current distorted pattern where regional governments finance over 80% of final payouts.
- **Rigorous Leakage Elimination and Social Audits** : Eliminating post-death disbursements and diversion of IEC funds requires institutionalising regular gram-sabha social audits alongside real-time civil registration data integration on the NSAP-PPS portal.
- **Streamlined Disability Onboarding** : States must operationalise the lowered 40% benchmark disability threshold by rolling out mobile certification camps, preventing administrative hurdles from excluding infants and young children newly eligible under the 2026 rules.


## Key Takeaways


- The Union Cabinet approved the Pradhan Mantri Samajik Sahayata Yojana on 14 October 2026 with a five-year outlay of ₹53,428 crore, extending the legacy NSAP architecture through FY 2030–31.
- Central monthly assistance for elderly beneficiaries aged 60 to 79 remains frozen at ₹200 per month, an amount that has seen zero upward revision since 2006–07.
- Disability pensions under the Pradhan Mantri Divyangjan Pension Yojana were raised by 25% to ₹375 per month, with eligibility widened by reducing the benchmark threshold from 80% to 40% and removing the 18-year age minimum.
- Beneficiary caps remain tethered to archaic Census 2001 parameters, expanding only marginally to 3.20 crore despite India's elderly demographic swelling to a projected 17.3 crore by 2026.
- States bear disproportionate fiscal pressure by financing 70% to more than 90% of total pension values, contributing top-ups ranging between ₹800 and ₹3,800 per month.
- The Supreme Court in Ashwani Kumar v. Union of India (2019) anchored the right of elderly individuals to live with dignity under Article 21, reinforcing the non-justiciable directive of Article 41.
